**Hydrogen – Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Typical Value / Description |
|----------|----------|-----------------------------|
| **Basic Identity** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| **Physical State at STP** | Phase | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.9 °C (120.2 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.2 °C (14 K) |
| | Density (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (ideal gas) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat (Cp) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.449 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Heat of fusion | 0.000 kJ mol⁻¹ (negligible) |
| | Enthalpy of formation (ΔH°f) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) |
| | Standard entropy (S°) | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy (ΔG°f) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Dipole moment | 0 (non‑polar) |
| | Polarizability | 0.666 × 10⁻²⁴ cm³ |
| | Van der Waals radius | 1.20 Å |
| | Covalent radius | 31 pm |
| | Atomic radius | 37 pm |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Bond length (H₂) | 0.74 Å |
| | Spectral lines | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series (UV, visible, IR) |
| **Chemical Behavior** | Oxidation state | +1 (in most compounds) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, etc. |
| | Reactivity | Highly flammable; reacts with O₂, N₂ (under catalysts), metals (forming hydrides). |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a proton donor (H⁺) in aqueous solution. |
| | Basic behavior | Forms hydride ions (H⁻) in metal hydrides. |
| | Redox potential (H⁺/H₂) | 0 V (standard hydrogen electrode). |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (≈0.0006 mol L⁻¹). |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Very low in non‑polar solvents; higher in polar aprotic solvents. |
| | Electrochemical properties | Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) are key in electrolysis. |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant (~99.98 %). |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, ~0.02 % natural abundance; heavier, lower zero‑point energy. |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β‑emitter, half‑life 12.32 y); used in nuclear fusion research. |
| | Isotopic effects | Deuterium forms stronger bonds (e.g., D₂O “heavy water”); affects reaction rates (kinetic isotope effect). |
| **Applications & Significance** | Energy carrier | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant, industrial hydrogenation. |
| | Nuclear fusion | Deuterium–tritium fusion (D-T) is the most studied reaction for future reactors. |
| | Analytical chemistry | Used as a standard in mass spectrometry, NMR (¹H NMR). |
| | Astrophysics | Hydrogen lines (e.g., Lyman‑α) are key in studying stellar spectra. |
| | Environmental science | Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) and methane (CH₄) are greenhouse gases; hydrogen is a clean alternative. |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Hydrogen is the simplest atom, with one proton and one electron.
- **Highly reactive**: Forms a wide variety of compounds; its diatomic form (H₂) is a powerful reducing agent.
- **Isotopic diversity**: Protium, deuterium, and tritium each have distinct physical and chemical properties, especially relevant in nuclear science.
- **Energy relevance**: Hydrogen is central to fuel cell technology and is a candidate for clean energy storage.
- **Spectroscopic importance**: Its spectral lines are foundational in astronomy and spectroscopy.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
